**Short answer.** The scattering of NAD(P)-binding enzymes across many SCOPe folds shows that NAD(P) binding has been invented independently several times (convergence), while the enormous functional diversity inside single superfamilies such as c.2.1 shows divergence from a common ancestor. Because the same cofactor can be bound by non-homologous folds, and because homologous domains can switch or lose cofactors, cofactor binding or active-site resemblance is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of common ancestry. Homology in SCOPe is asserted at the superfamily level only when structural similarity is accompanied by shared features that the chemistry does not require.

**What the SCOPe hierarchy means at each level.** Family (e.g. c.2.1.2 tyrosine-dependent/SDR oxidoreductases, c.2.1.1 alcohol-dehydrogenase C-terminal domain, c.2.1.3 GAPDH-like N-terminal domain, c.2.1.4 formate/glycerate dehydrogenase NAD domain, c.2.1.6 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase-like N-terminal domain) = clear common ancestry supported by sequence similarity or very close structure/function. Superfamily (c.2.1 NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains) = probable common ancestry inferred from shared structural and functional features even where sequences have diverged beyond detection. Fold (c.2) = same core secondary-structure arrangement and topology, with no claim of homology. Class (c, alpha/beta) = secondary-structure composition only. Only family and superfamily assignments are evolutionary statements; fold and class membership can be shared by analogues.

**Where NAD(P) binding occurs in SCOPe.** Distinct folds that bind NAD(P) (or NAD as substrate) include: c.2 (Rossmann fold, parallel 6-stranded sheet, order 321456, superfamily c.2.1: SDRs, MDRs, GAPDH, LDH/MDH, 6PGDH, UDP-glucose DH, amino-acid DH C-terminal domains); c.3 (FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain, c.3.1: glutathione reductase and related flavoprotein disulfide reductases, succinate dehydrogenase flavoprotein N-terminal domain, with a 5-stranded parallel core order 32145 plus an antiparallel beta-meander); c.4 (Nucleotide-binding domain, c.4.1); c.25 (Ferredoxin reductase-like C-terminal NADP-linked domain, c.25.1, paired with the all-beta FAD-binding domain b.43.4); c.31 (DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding domain, c.31.1, containing deoxyhypusine synthase, the sirtuin/Sir2 family that consumes NAD+ as a co-substrate, transhydrogenase dIII and pyruvate oxidase middle domains); c.71 (Dihydrofolate reductase-like, c.71.1, NADPH on a mixed 8-stranded sheet); c.77 (Isocitrate/isopropylmalate dehydrogenase-like, c.77.1, NAD(P) bound in a non-Rossmann mode); c.82 (ALDH-like, c.82.1, duplicated Rossmann-like domains with a non-canonical NAD pose); c.1 TIM barrel, superfamily c.1.7 (NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductases, the aldo-keto reductases, NADPH in an extended conformation at the C-terminal end of the barrel); d.166 (ADP-ribosylation fold, d.166.1: diphtheria toxin, pertussis toxin S1, PARP catalytic domains, which cleave NAD+ rather than use it for hydride transfer); and c.26.1 (adenine-nucleotide alpha-hydrolase-like, which holds NAD synthetase and NMN adenylyltransferase that make NAD). These are placed in different folds because their core topologies differ, not merely because they bind different ligands.

**Convergence versus divergence.** (1) Convergence: NAD(P) is an ancient, abundant ligand with a limited set of physically favourable binding modes. The beta-alpha-beta crossover unit whose first-helix N-terminus (with a GxGxxG-type glycine-rich loop) cradles the pyrophosphate is a generic solution for nucleotide binding, and it recurs in c.2, c.3, c.4, c.31 and, in a different guise, P-loop NTPases (c.37). SCOPe curators therefore keep c.2 and c.3 as separate folds even though both have a Rossmann-like ADP-binding unit and a glycine motif: the rest of the topology (the extra antiparallel meander in c.3, the different strand order) is not derivable from the shared unit. The TIM-barrel aldo-keto reductases (c.1.7), DHFR (c.71), ICDH (c.77) and ADP-ribosyltransferases (d.166) are clear-cut independent inventions of NAD(P) recognition on unrelated scaffolds. The same NAD can even be used with opposite hydride stereochemistry (pro-R versus pro-S face) by different dehydrogenases, reinforcing that cofactor use is a chemical constraint rather than an evolutionary fingerprint. (2) Divergence: inside c.2.1 the sequences of SDRs, MDRs, GAPDH and LDH are not detectably similar, substrates range from alcohols to amino acids to sugars, and the nicotinamide half of the site is built by different additional subdomains, yet the superfamily shares the full six-strand topology, the glycine-rich loop at the same position, and the conserved acidic residue at the C-terminus of beta2 that hydrogen-bonds the adenosine 2'-OH (replaced by basic residues in NADP-specific members). Those shared idiosyncrasies, together with intermediate sequences linking families, justify a single superfamily and a divergent interpretation.

**Why cofactor or active-site similarity alone is insufficient.** (a) Functional constraints are strong enough to produce the same local solution independently: the classic parallel is the Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad that arose separately in trypsin-like (b.47), subtilisin-like (c.41) and alpha/beta-hydrolase (c.69) folds. Any feature that selection would reproduce in any fold cannot discriminate homology from analogy. (b) The converse also holds: homologous domains can lose or change the ligand. Rossmann-type domains within c.2 and related superfamilies bind FAD, CoA, SAM-like nucleotides or no cofactor at all, and NAD versus NADP preference can flip with one or two substitutions at the end of beta2. Cofactor identity is therefore neither necessary nor sufficient. (c) The Rossmann fold is a superfold: many non-homologous proteins adopt it because it is a highly favourable alpha/beta architecture, so structure superposition scores (DALI Z, TM-score) for a Rossmann-like pair must be judged against the high background of that fold, not against random structures. (d) Same ligand, different chemistry: sirtuins (c.31.1), ADP-ribosyltransferases (d.166.1) and dehydrogenases (c.2.1) all bind NAD+ but catalyse deacetylation, ADP-ribosyl transfer and hydride transfer respectively, with no shared catalytic residues.

**Evidence that would support homology instead.** Statistically significant sequence or profile-profile/HMM similarity (including transitive links through intermediate sequences); conservation of specific residues at structurally equivalent positions that are not required by the chemistry; shared unusual topological features (strand order, crossover connections, insertions) beyond the generic beta-alpha-beta unit; structural similarity well above the fold-specific background; conserved domain architecture, gene fusions or genomic context; and phylogenetic analysis consistent with a single origin. SCOPe superfamily assignments encode exactly this combination, and SCOPe release notes (SCOPe 2.07/2.08) retain the c.2 versus c.3 versus c.31 separation on that basis.

**Practical limits.** Do not transfer NAD versus NADP specificity, catalytic residues or substrate range across folds, and be cautious even across families within c.2.1; check the beta2 acidic/basic residue and the nicotinamide-binding subdomain directly. For template selection (e.g. from ASTRAL representative sets), choose a template from the same family or at least the same superfamily; a template that merely shares the Rossmann fold (or only the GxGxxG motif) cannot be assumed to share the ligand pose, the hydride-transfer face or the active-site residues. Any functional annotation inferred from cofactor binding alone should be flagged as low-confidence until independent sequence-profile, conserved-residue or genomic-context evidence is obtained.
